drafts.title: 22%. That's how much range an EV can lose near freezing. I cross the Rockies this weekend (pack AP3, EV first-hand)
drafts.window: Sat ~5-6 PM (bright cell), as Day 1 of the drive wraps. If Sat is the scoreboard post, move this to Sun ~1 AM or post as a reply under it.
drafts.angle: The drive home goes over the Rockies on I-70 in late October. Honest "here's what cold does and what I do about it." No fear, no specs. Sets up the Rockies payoff post. OCR note: OK to Strong. Cold range is the top worry for people on the fence, and "I'll post the real numbers" brings them back for the payoff.
bullets: Near 32 F an EV can lose about 22% of its range, mostly from heating the cabin and a cold battery (Selectra test summary, U.K.; same physics here).
Easy fixes: warm it up while still plugged in, use seat and wheel heat instead of blasting the cabin, check tire pressure, plan a bigger buffer.
Tesla nav warms the battery on the way to a Supercharger so it charges faster in the cold.
Fill-ins for the payoff post: [% at the bottom ___ / % at the top ___ / outside temp ___].
drafts.body:
SHORT VERSION:
22%.

That's how much range an EV can lose near freezing.

This weekend I drive home over the Rockies in late October.

My plan: warm it up while it's still plugged in, seat heat instead of cabin heat, and a bigger buffer than I think I need.

I'll post the real numbers from the top. What's your cold-weather trick?

LONGER FRAMEWORK:
22%. That's how much range an electric car can lose when it's around freezing. Most of it goes to keeping you warm, not moving the car.

I'm about to find out for myself. Sunday I climb the Rockies on I-70 heading home to Grand Junction.

Here's what I'm doing: warm the car while it's still on the charger so the wall pays for the heat, not the battery. Heated seat and wheel instead of cranking the cabin. Tires checked. And I'll charge a little higher than the car says I need.

I'll post what the battery read at the bottom and the top. Old-timers who drive EVs in snow country, what's your trick?

drafts.title: $3 billion. That's what people 60+ reported losing to scams last year. Two free fixes (pack AP5, AI for normal people, 55+)
drafts.window: Tue ~1-3 PM (strongest weekday block), or a Thu ~8 PM Pixel video version.
drafts.angle: Fresh FTC numbers give a dollar opener for the safe-word story he already lived. Replaces Thu's safe-word item (not posted). Kind tone, no shaming victims. OCR note: Strong. Big dollar, two concrete free steps, and a question aimed at 35-54 sons and daughters that lands with 55+ too. Very saveable.
bullets: FTC report to Congress: Americans 60+ reported about $3 billion in fraud losses in 2025, up 25% from $2.4B in 2024 and up 400% from $600M in 2020 (CNBC, Oct 22).
Only 6% lost $100,000 or more, but they were 70% of the losses. FTC estimates the real total with unreported losses could be $13.3B to $119.5B.
Investment scams cost the most (over $1B, up 42%), then government impersonation ($448M) and business impersonation ($422M).
Free fix 1: a family safe word (his cloned-voice catch https://x.com/UpgradeAmerican/status/2112703584488005681). Free fix 2: a "trusted contact" on your bank or brokerage account.
Medicare open enrollment runs to Dec 7, a busy season for fake "Medicare" calls (CMS).
drafts.body:
SHORT VERSION:
$3 billion.

That's what people 60 and older reported losing to scams last year. Up 25%.

Two free fixes I did:
A family safe word.
A trusted contact on my bank account.

Took about 10 minutes. Have you set these up for your parents?

LONGER FRAMEWORK:
$3 billion. That's just what people 60 and up reported losing to scams last year. The FTC thinks the real number is a lot bigger because most people never report it.

A few weeks ago I heard a voice that sounded right and wasn't. I caught it because I spent 20 years running sound. Most people won't have that.

So here are two free things that work no matter how good the fake sounds:
A family safe word. If someone calls in a panic, ask for it.
A trusted contact at your bank. If something looks off, they call that person before your money moves.

And if it happens to someone you love, don't say "how could you." They already feel it.

Have you set this up for your parents yet?
